hotlines.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
hotlines.description: Confidential support, safety planning, and local resources for anyone experiencing domestic violence.

hotlines.name: Crisis Text Line
hotlines.description: Free, confidential crisis counseling via text message. Available for any emotional crisis.

hotlines.name: RAINN National Sexual Assault Hotline
hotlines.description: Confidential support from trained staff. Routes callers to local affiliate sexual assault service providers.

hotlines.name: loveisrespect (Teen Dating Violence)
hotlines.description: Peer advocates for young people experiencing dating abuse. Highly trained, non-judgmental support.

hotlines.name: National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI)
hotlines.description: Mental health support, resources, and education for those affected by mental illness, including trauma from abuse.

hotlines.name: National Human Trafficking Hotline
hotlines.description: Support and resources for trafficking victims and survivors, and to report tips.

hotlines.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
hotlines.description: Domestic, dating, and sexual violence helpline for Native Americans and Alaska Natives.

hotlines.name: LGBT National Hotline
hotlines.description: Peer support for LGBT community members dealing with relationship abuse, coming out, and other challenges.

hotlines.name: National Alliance for Eating Disorders
hotlines.description: Support for those suffering from eating disorders, which can co-occur with or be exacerbated by abusive relationships.

educational.title: What Is Emotional Abuse?
educational.summary: Emotional abuse is a pattern of behavior that harms a person's emotional health and sense of self-worth. Unlike physical violence, it leaves no visible marks — which can make it harder to recognize and harder for others to validate.

body.heading: The core of emotional abuse
body.text: Emotional abuse is defined by its pattern, not by individual incidents. One harsh argument isn't abuse. A sustained campaign of control, humiliation, manipulation, and isolation is. Abusers use psychological tactics to make their targets feel confused, worthless, or dependent.

body.heading: It's about power and control
body.text: Every tactic in emotional abuse serves the same goal: to maintain the abuser's power over the target. Gaslighting makes you doubt your reality. Isolation removes your support. Ultimatums force compliance. Love bombing resets the cycle. These aren't random outbursts — they're a system.

body.heading: Why it's hard to recognize
body.text: Emotional abuse often escalates slowly. By the time it's severe, you've already normalized much of it. The abuser frequently frames their behavior as love, concern, or your fault. Many survivors don't identify their experience as abuse until they are safely out.

body.heading: It's not your fault
body.text: Nothing you did, said, or failed to say caused the abuse. Abusers choose their behavior. Healthy relationships have conflict — they don't have control. If you feel like you're always walking on eggshells, that feeling is data.

educational.title: Understanding Gaslighting
educational.summary: Gaslighting is a form of psychological manipulation in which an abuser causes a target to question their own memory, perception, and sanity. The term comes from the 1944 film 'Gaslight,' in which a husband dims the gas lights and denies it when his wife notices.

body.heading: How it works
body.text: The abuser systematically denies events, contradicts your memories, trivializes your feelings, and redirects blame. Over time, you stop trusting your own perception and start relying on the abuser's version of reality — which is exactly the goal.

body.heading: Common phrases
body.text: "You're imagining things." "I never said that." "You're too sensitive." "You're crazy." "Everyone else thinks you overreact." "That's not what happened." These phrases, used repeatedly, erode your confidence in your own mind.

body.heading: The long-term damage
body.text: Chronic gaslighting can lead to anxiety, depression, and PTSD. Survivors often describe feeling like they 'can't trust themselves' even after leaving the relationship. Recovery involves rebuilding trust in your own perceptions — a process that therapy can accelerate significantly.

body.heading: Grounding yourself
body.text: If you suspect you're being gaslit: keep a private journal of events as they happen. Note dates, words used, and how you felt. This creates an external record to counter the internal confusion. Trusted friends and therapists can also serve as reality checks.

educational.title: The Cycle of Abuse
educational.summary: Most abusive relationships follow a predictable pattern known as the 'cycle of abuse,' described by researcher Lenore Walker in 1979. Understanding this cycle is often what finally helps survivors recognize their situation.

body.heading: Phase 1: Tension building
body.text: Stress increases. The abuser becomes irritable, demanding, and unpredictable. The target walks on eggshells, trying to manage the abuser's moods and avoid triggering an outburst. This phase can last days, weeks, or months.

body.heading: Phase 2: The incident
body.text: The abusive episode occurs — verbal attacks, threats, manipulation, or physical violence. The abuser may seem to 'snap' or act with cold deliberateness. Afterward, the target is often in shock, confusion, or fear.

body.heading: Phase 3: Reconciliation (the 'honeymoon')
body.text: The abuser apologizes, makes promises, or minimizes what happened. They may be unusually loving, attentive, or generous. This is the 'love bombing' phase. It gives the target hope that the relationship can be what it was — or what they believed it could be.

body.heading: Phase 4: Calm
body.text: A period of relative peace follows, during which the target may doubt the severity of what happened. But the cycle always repeats. Each cycle often escalates in severity over time.

body.heading: Why people stay
body.text: The cycle creates powerful psychological bonds. Intermittent reinforcement (alternating punishment and reward) is one of the strongest conditioning mechanisms known. It's not weakness that keeps people in abusive relationships — it's neurochemistry, fear, financial dependence, love, and hope.

educational.title: Coercive Control
educational.summary: Coercive control is a pattern of behavior that seeks to take away the victim's liberty or freedom. It's the framework underlying most sustained abuse — and in several countries and U.S. states, it's now a criminal offense.

body.heading: What it looks like
body.text: Monitoring your location, finances, communications, and social life. Making you ask permission. Controlling what you wear or eat. Isolating you from friends and family. Creating financial dependence. Using children as leverage. These behaviors, individually, may seem trivial. As a pattern, they constitute a cage.

body.heading: The goal
body.text: Unlike a single incident of violence, coercive control is ongoing. Its goal isn't to hurt you once — it's to dominate your life continuously. Survivors often report that the control itself was more damaging than any individual incident.

body.heading: Digital coercive control
body.text: Modern abusers use technology: tracking apps, demanding passwords, monitoring social media, flooding phones with messages, using smart home devices to create confusion or discomfort. If your partner uses technology to monitor or control you, that is abuse.

body.heading: Legal landscape
body.text: As of 2024, coercive control laws exist in the UK, Ireland, Scotland, Australia, and several U.S. states including California, Connecticut, and Hawaii. More states are considering legislation. Document patterns carefully — screenshots, dates, descriptions.

educational.title: Leaving Safely
educational.summary: Leaving an abusive relationship is often the most dangerous period for a victim. The risk of violence escalates when an abuser believes they are losing control. Safety planning before and during leaving is critical.

body.heading: Before you leave
body.text: Build a safety plan with a domestic violence advocate before acting. Gather copies of important documents (ID, passport, birth certificate, financial records) and store them somewhere safe, ideally outside the home. Set aside emergency cash if possible.

body.heading: Trusted people
body.text: Identify 2-3 trusted people who know your situation and can help. Create a code word you can text or say that means 'call 911' or 'come get me.' Don't rely on a single escape route.

body.heading: Your devices
body.text: Abusers often monitor devices. Use a private browser or a device your abuser doesn't have access to when researching resources. Clear your browser history afterward. Change passwords from a device they can't access. Disable location sharing.

body.heading: Children and pets
body.text: Abusers often use children and pets as leverage. Contact a DV hotline to understand your legal rights before taking any action involving children. Many shelters now accommodate pets.

body.heading: After leaving
body.text: Leaving doesn't end the risk immediately. Change locks, inform trusted neighbors, notify your workplace, and consider a protective order. The National Domestic Violence Hotline can help with all of these steps.

educational.title: Healing & Recovery
educational.summary: Recovery from emotional abuse is real and possible. It is also nonlinear, deeply personal, and takes longer than most people expect — but survivors consistently report that life after abuse can be genuinely good.

body.heading: What recovery looks like
body.text: Recovery isn't a straight line. You may have good weeks followed by setbacks. Anniversaries, songs, smells, or places can trigger grief or fear. This is normal. It doesn't mean you're 'not over it' — it means your nervous system is healing.

body.heading: Therapy modalities that help
body.text: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) is highly effective for trauma. CBT (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy) helps reframe distorted beliefs the abuse installed. Somatic therapies address the physical dimension of trauma that 'lives in the body.' Look for a therapist who specializes in trauma or domestic abuse.

body.heading: Rebuilding self-trust
body.text: Emotional abuse systematically destroys self-trust. A major part of recovery is learning to trust your own perceptions again. Start small: notice a feeling, name it, act on it. Journal. Practice making small decisions independently. Every time you trust yourself and it works out, you're rebuilding.

body.heading: Community
body.text: Peer support groups (in-person and online) connect you with survivors who understand what you've been through without you having to explain. Organizations like the National DV Hotline, RAINN, and loveisrespect have referral networks for local support groups.

body.heading: You were not broken by this
body.text: The abuse changed you — but it did not break you. Survivors demonstrate extraordinary resilience, creativity, and empathy. The same skills you used to navigate an abusive relationship are strengths. You survived. That is not nothing.
